traces.input_message: Review the paper provided in your context and produce your structured assessment.
traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply calibrated skepticism: hold the paper to the venue's real acceptance bar, where most submissions are rejected. Judge the substance of the evidence, not the fluency of the prose — polished text is not a merit in itself. Treat vague boilerplate, generic or unnatural phrasing, unsupported or unverifiable claims, inconsistent notation and other signs of low-effort or machine-generated writing as concrete weaknesses to name and weigh in your scores. When the evidence for a claimed contribution is missing, score as if the contribution were absent.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: The paper introduces a 2k-message, four-label (Satisfaction, Frustration, Caution, Neutral) dataset for developer emotion in GitHub commits, reports near-chance zero-shot results, fine-tunes CodeBERT to Macro-F1≈0.59, and proposes CommiTune: LLaMA-based paraphrase augmentation followed by CodeBERT fine-tuning, achieving Macro-F1≈0.82 on a 400-sample test set. Annotation and sampling pipelines are described; code/data promised on acceptance.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: A focused SE-EMO dataset and a simple hybrid augmentation pipeline for commit messages are useful and practically relevant. However, novelty is modest and the empirical methodology has gaps that weaken the strength of the claimed advance.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.3: Clear, iterative annotation with κ improving from 0.596 to 0.710 and a domain-appropriate four-label scheme, including the useful Caution category.
Sections 4–5: Baselines (zero-shot and fine-tuned) are established and show a real gap that domain adaptation can address.
Section 5.2: CommiTune yields large, consistent gains, notably fixing Satisfaction (F1 from 0.46 to 0.77), suggesting practical utility for SE NLP.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 4.4.1: The claim that LLaMA’s “classification head is resized for four outputs” is architecturally inconsistent for a generative LM and undermines technical clarity/soundness.
Section 4.2: Applying a lexicon-based override (forcing Caution) inside zero-shot evaluation biases comparisons and weakens the claim that LLMs fail in an unbiased setting.

Sections 4.4–5.2: No ablations (e.g., back-translation, off-the-shelf paraphrasers, class rebalancing, augmentation without LLaMA fine-tuning), leaving the source of the large +0.23 Macro-F1 gain insufficiently supported.

Sections 3.3, 4.3, 5: Missing key details (class distribution, validation split for baseline fine-tuning, seed/variance, cross-project/OOD tests) and visible formatting glitches (e.g., “321 5.1”) reduce reproducibility and clarity.
suggestions: Section 5.2: Provide qualitative examples of augmented paraphrases with human checks for label fidelity to illustrate augmentation quality.
Section 6: Add a brief ethics/use section on monitoring developer emotion and potential misuse.
Section 3.1–3.3: Include a concise summary table with class distributions and guideline snippets to aid reuse.

response_payload.summary: The paper introduces a 2,000-example, human-labeled dataset of GitHub commit messages with a four-label scheme (Satisfaction, Frustration, Caution, Neutral), shows zero-shot models perform near chance, and proposes CommiTune: fine-tune a LLaMA generator to augment data, then retrain CodeBERT, reaching Macro-F1 ≈ 0.82 and Acc ≈ 0.81 on a 400-sample test set. The annotation pipeline raises κ from 0.596 to 0.710, and the largest gain is on Satisfaction (F1 0.46→0.77).
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: A focused, domain-adapted affect dataset and taxonomy (adding Caution) plus a simple hybrid augmentation pipeline yield large gains over baselines. Novelty is moderate: the dataset/taxonomy are new in this domain; augmentation with LLMs is known but applied effectively here.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.3 details a rigorous annotation and reconciliation process, raising κ from 0.596 to 0.710 and introducing the domain-relevant Caution label.
Section 5 establishes clear diagnostics: zero-shot baselines perform poorly (Macro-F1 0.13–0.21), and a fine-tuned CodeBERT reaches Macro-F1 ≈ 0.59, quantifying the challenge.
Section 5.2/Table 3 show large, consistent gains from CommiTune (Macro-F1 ≈ 0.82; Acc ≈ 0.81), notably boosting Satisfaction F1 from 0.46 to 0.77.
Introduction and Section 5 document systematic biases of zero-shot models on technical jargon, motivating domain adaptation.
reasons_for_rejection: Sections 1 and 5.2 describe CommiTune but omit key methodological details (prompt templates, generation volume, filtering criteria, deduplication), limiting reproducibility and interpretability of the gains.

Section 5.2 evaluates on the same 400-sample test set but provides no safeguards against synthetic–test overlap or repository-level leakage, leaving open the possibility that augmentation contaminated evaluation.

Section 5 lacks ablations isolating augmentation effects (e.g., varying synthetic size/ratios, alternative augmenters like backtranslation noted in Section 2.4, or synthetic-only training), so the source of improvements is unclear.
Sections 5 and 5.2 report single-run point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests, so the robustness of Macro-F1 ≈ 0.82 is not established.
suggestions: Section 3.3: Release full annotation guidelines, reconciliation scripts, and a data card with license and class distributions to aid reuse.
Section 5: Add qualitative error analyses with representative commit snippets per class to complement confusion matrices.
Section 5: Report calibration metrics (e.g., ECE/Brier) for EmoLLaMA-7B to substantiate the ‘poorly calibrated’ claim.
Section 6: Expand on ethical considerations and safeguards for any deployment in developer well-being monitoring.

response_payload.summary: Introduces a 2,000-example, 4-label (Satisfaction/Frustration/Caution/Neutral) commit-message emotion dataset; shows zero-shot baselines near chance (Macro-F1 0.13–0.21). Fine-tuned CodeBERT reaches ≈0.59 Macro-F1. Proposes CommiTune: fine-tune LLaMA, generate augmented data, then fine-tune CodeBERT, achieving ≈0.82 Macro-F1 (≈0.81 Acc) on a 400-example test split.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Valuable domain-specific dataset and a practical hybrid augmentation pipeline for SE affect detection. Methodological novelty is modest; main contribution is empirical validation that LLM-based augmentation markedly boosts a code-aware encoder.
reasons_for_acceptance: 5 Results: CommiTune improves Macro-F1 from the CodeBERT baseline (~0.59) to ~0.82 on the held-out test, a large and practically meaningful gain.
4.1 Baselines and 5 Results: A reasonably broad set of baselines (NLI zero-shot, emotion-tuned, code-aware, LLaMA) is evaluated with Macro-F1 and accuracy.
Introduction: The task is well-motivated for developer well-being and software reliability, and the 4-label taxonomy appears domain-appropriate.
Introduction and IAA claim: The annotation/reconciliation pipeline raises κ from 0.596 to 0.710, indicating solid labeling quality.
reasons_for_rejection: 4.4 CommiTune and 4.4.3 Final Training: Insufficient detail on augmentation prompts, label-preservation, filtering, and synthetic data quality control prevents assessing validity and reproducibility.

5 Results and 4 Experimental Setup: No ablations (e.g., augmentation volume, LLaMA vs other generators), no multi-seed variance/confidence intervals, and a single 1600/400 split undermine robustness claims.
5 Results/Table 1 and 4.2 Zero-shot: Zero-shot scores below random Macro-F1 (0.25) without prompt/mapping specifics suggest possible unfair evaluation or miscalibration.
Presentation: Duplicated Abstracts, formatting glitches (spacing in κ values), and cross-references to missing subsections (e.g., 4.3 details) reduce clarity and raise concern about completeness.
suggestions: Provide dataset/model cards with licensing, taxonomy, and reconciliation guidelines to ease adoption.
Include qualitative examples per class with brief rationales to illustrate subtle cues in commit messages.
Release scripts for zero-shot prompt templates and label mappings plus confusion-matrix plots for diagnostics.
Report stratified performance by message length or repository to guide deployment settings.

You are the meta-reviewer of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the individual peer reviews of one submission and synthesize them into a single aggregated assessment for the Area Chair.

Structure your synthesis in this order:
1. Points of consensus among the reviewers.
2. Disagreements, and which side is better supported.
3. The decisive strengths and weaknesses after weighing the arguments.

Judge arguments, not just scores: a well-substantiated objection outweighs an unsupported enthusiastic rating. Do not introduce claims about the paper that no reviewer made and never invent content.

Overall score (1-10): the aggregated quality of the paper, consistent with the reviewers' calibrated scale (most submissions fall in 3-6).
Recommendation: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).

Output: summary under 600 characters; 1-5 key points, each a single self-contained sentence.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

While the dataset/taxonomy appear useful, the empirical evidence is not sufficiently rigorous for ICLR.
key_points: All reviewers value the new 2k commit-message dataset and four-label taxonomy (including Caution) and note improved IAA (κ 0.596→0.710).
Reported gains from CommiTune over a CodeBERT baseline are large (Macro-F1 ~0.59→~0.82) on a 400-sample test set.
There is consensus that key methodological details and ablations are missing (augmentation prompts/filters, size ratios, seeds/variance), undermining reproducibility and causal attribution.
Reviewers raise concerns about evaluation validity, including possible synthetic–test or repository leakage and biased or unfair zero-shot setups (e.g., lexicon override, below-random F1).
A claim about resizing LLaMA’s classification head is flagged by one reviewer and, while less corroborated, highlights presentation/technical clarity issues that must be fixed.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

Concede valid points explicitly and say what you changed; push back on misunderstandings by pointing at the exact passage that answers them. Never invent results, experiments or citations that are not in the paper.

Only reference sections, numbers and results you have actually seen. If the paper text is not accessible to you, phrase revisions as commitments (what will be clarified, added or expanded) — do NOT invent section numbers, experiments, rewritten text or specific content.

Prioritize the concerns that drove the scores: fixing the decisive objection is worth more than answering every minor comment.

Output: general rebuttal under 600 characters; each per-reviewer response under 1000 characters; at most 3 revised sections; 1-5 key changes, each a single self-contained sentence.

response_payload.rebuttal: We appreciate the reviews and AC. We concede that parts of our evaluation and reporting lacked rigor and detail (zero-shot setup, leakage controls, ablations, and reproducibility). We clarify that no test data were ever used for augmentation or tuning, remove the zero-shot lexicon override, add strict leakage checks and split protocols, and commit comprehensive ablations and full artifact release. The revised sections below reflect these changes and improve transparency.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: Concern: leakage and split validity. Clarification: Augmentation used only training commits (4.4.2: “generate two paraphrases for each training commit”), and the held-out test split was never used for model selection (4.4.3). We acknowledge that we did not describe leakage controls sufficiently and that our 80/20 split on augmented data for validation could be clearer. Changes: (i) corpus-level de-duplication before splitting; (ii) semantic similarity filtering of synthetic data against dev/test; (iii) validation drawn only from the original training set; (iv) fixed seeds and repository-/time-aware splits added as robustness checks. We will report both random-stratified and repo/time-holdout results (without claiming new numbers here). We will release commit/message IDs for all splits.

Concern: biased zero-shot setup and mapping validity. We agree our lexicon-based override for Caution may bias comparisons; we have removed it and now use a uniform protocol. Revisions to §4.2: (i) multiple prompt templates per model with majority vote; (ii) standardized hypothesis templates for MNLI; (iii) consistent preprocessing across models; (iv) explicit label mapping tables; (v) no test-time calibration or threshold tuning; (vi) report random and majority-class baselines and confidence intervals. We will include all prompts, mappings, and scripts in the artifact to ensure reproduci bility and fair zero-shot comparisons.

Concern: missing ablations and insufficient reproducibility detail. We concur. Revisions: We add an ablation plan isolating each factor: (a) CodeBERT on gold only; (b) +backtranslation; (c) +off-the-shelf LLaMA paraphrases; (d) +fine-tuned LLaMA paraphrases; (e) synthetic-only; (f) mixing ratios and loss weighting; (g) number of paraphrases; (h) removal of potential near-duplicates. We will report per-class metrics, 95% bootstrap CIs, and McNemar tests vs. the primary baseline. We also add exact preprocessing, split IDs, seeds, and training scripts, plus annotation guidelines and reconciliation rules for full reproducibility.

revised_sections.content:
All experiments use the 2,000-message gold-standard dataset with a fixed held-out test split of 400 examples; the remaining 1,600 form the training pool. A validation set is drawn exclusively from the training pool and used for early stopping and model selection; the test set is never used for tuning.
Leakage controls. Before splitting, we perform corpus-level de-duplication (exact-match and normalized variants). Synthetic data are generated only from training messages. We filter synthetic outputs that are near-duplicates of any dev/test message (semantic similarity and hash-based checks) and remove duplicates within the training set. We fix random seeds and will release split IDs for full reproducibility. In addition to stratified random splits, we report robustness checks with (i) repository-holdout and (ii) temporally separated splits (train earlier, test later) to assess generalization under distribution shift.
Metrics and statistics. We report Macro-F1, per-class precision/recall/F1, and accuracy. We provide 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and conduct McNemar tests for paired comparisons to the primary baseline. All preprocessing, training, and evaluation scripts (including seed control) will be released in an anonymized artifact.
Baselines. We evaluate five pretrained models spanning general-purpose reasoning, code-aware representation, and emotion-focused classification (as listed previously). We ensure identical preprocessing across models and no heuristic overrides.
Fine-tuning. For fine-tuned baselines, the classification head is a four-way softmax. Early stopping and model selection use the validation set only. Hyperparameters and seeds are fixed and documented in the artifact.

We evaluate all baselines in a uniform zero-shot framework without any heuristic overrides. For RoBERTa-large-MNLI, we pair each commit (premise) with standardized hypothesis templates (e.g., “This commit expresses {label}.”) and select the label with the highest entailment score; we also include logically equivalent variants and aggregate by majority vote. For emotion-tuned classifiers, we map fine-grained emotions to our four labels using an explicit, published mapping table. For generative models, we use an ensemble of prompt templates instructing four-class classification; outputs are normalized and aggregated by majority vote.
No component is tuned on the test set, and prompts/templates are fixed prior to evaluation. We report performance with identical preprocessing across models, alongside random and majority-class baselines and 95% CIs. All prompts, mappings, and normalization scripts will be released.

CommiTune is a two-stage pipeline: (1) fine-tune a generative LLaMA model on the 1,600 training commits to align with the four-label taxonomy; (2) use it to synthesize paraphrases only for training commits, then fine-tune CodeBERT on the union of gold and filtered synthetic data.
Stage 1 (generator fine-tuning). We adapt Meta-LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct using PEFT/LoRA. Training uses the 1,600 training commits, a four-way output space, and early stopping on the validation set; no test information is used. Exact seeds and configuration are provided in the artifact.
Stage 2 (augmentation and filtering). For each training commit, the generator produces paraphrases conditioned on the gold label. We then: (i) remove duplicates and enforce single-sentence formatting; (ii) discard outputs whose semantic similarity to the seed is too low (to avoid label drift) or too high (to avoid trivial copies); (iii) filter out any synthetic instance that is near-duplicate to any dev/test message (to prevent leakage). We upweight gold data during training via sampling/loss weighting (documented in the artifact).
Final training. CodeBERT is fine-tuned on the combined dataset with early stopping on the validation set drawn from gold data. Seeds, hyperparameters, and training scripts are fixed and released.
Ablations and controls. We will report: CodeBERT on gold only; +backtranslation; +off-the-shelf LLaMA paraphrases; +fine-tuned LLaMA paraphrases; synthetic-only; varying the number of paraphrases and mixing policies; and removal of potential near-duplicates. We include per-class metrics, 95% CIs, and McNemar tests versus the gold-only baseline.

key_changes: Removed the lexicon-based override and standardized a fair, model-agnostic zero-shot protocol with prompt ensembles and explicit mappings.
Added rigorous leakage controls: corpus-level de-duplication, semantic filtering against dev/test, fixed seeds, and repository/time-aware robustness splits.
Clarified train/validation/test usage, with early stopping only on validation derived from training and no test-time tuning.
Specified a comprehensive ablation suite isolating augmentation source, quantity, and mixing, with confidence intervals and statistical tests.
Committed to releasing anonymized code, prompts, split IDs, seeds, and annotation guidelines to ensure full reproducibility.
